items.title: Come trasformare un MacBook inutilizzato in un NAS domestico
items.summary: Lunità può essere utilizzata per archiviazione e backup.
items.content:
Anche un MacBook con qualche anno alle spalle può trovare una seconda vita all'interno della rete domestica, trasformandosi in un piccolo server per archiviare file, effettuare backup o riprodurre contenuti multimediali. L'operazione richiede pochi passaggi e può essere effettuata sfruttando macOS, con un investimento minimo o pari a zero.

MACOS È LA SOLUZIONE PIÙ SEMPLICE

Il primo passo da compiere per poter sfruttare il proprio MacBook come NAS (Network Attached Storage) o hub domestico è quello di formattare l'unità per riportarlo alle impostazioni di fabbrica. Il consiglio è chiaramente quello di utilizzare l'ultima versione del sistema operativo disponibile per il modello in proprio possesso.

Grazie alle funzioni integrate di macOS, non è indispensabile installare un sistema operativo alternativo. La strada più immediata consiste, infatti, nell'attivare l'opzione di condivisione file, raggiungibile nelle impostazioni di sistema. Qui è possibile scegliere quali cartelle rendere disponibili sulla rete e stabilire quali utenti possono accedervi, oltre a fornire l'indirizzo IP.

items.title: Benzina dall'aria? Il sistema di questa startup ne produce 3,8 litri al giorno
items.summary: Una startup newyorkese ha presentato un dispositivo in grado di trasformare anidride carbonica e acqua in carburante sintetico per i motori tradizionali.
items.content:
L'aumento dei prezzi della benzina e del gasolio alla pompa continua a pesare sul bilancio di famiglie ed imprese, riaccendendo il dibattito sulla dipendenza dai combustibili fossili e sulla necessità di accelerare verso soluzioni energetiche innovative. In questo scenario di forti tensioni sui listini dei carburanti tradizionali, riscuote interesse la proposta tecnologica avanzata dalla startup newyorkese Aircela. L'azienda ha svelato un dispositivo compatto, dalle dimensioni simili a quelle di un frigorifero americano, capace di produrre benzina direttamente dall'aria, dall'acqua e dall'energia elettrica rinnovabile, offrendo un carburante sintetico immediatamente utilizzabile nelle auto già in circolazione.

Come funziona la tecnologia: dalla CO2 alla benzina

Il sistema sviluppato da Aircela unisce tre distinti processi chimici in una struttura modulare formata da tre elementi esagonali interconnessi. Nella prima fase del processo viene catturata l'anidride carbonica presente nell'aria atmosferica mediante una soluzione liquida a base di idrossido di potassio. Successivamente, un elettrolizzatore alimentato da elettricità rinnovabile scinde l'acqua per ottenere idrogeno, rilasciando ossigeno nell'ambiente. Infine, l'anidride carbonica e l'idrogeno vengono combinati per sintetizzare metanolo, poi convertito in benzina sintetica pronta all'uso tramite un processo noto come "methanol-to-gasoline". Il carburante ottenuto è privo di zolfo, etanolo e metalli pesanti, ed è compatibile con i serbatoi, le pompe ed i motori a combustione esistenti senza richiedere modifiche.

Produzione di 3,8 litri al giorno

Il dispositivo mostrato da Aircela è in grado di produrre circa un gallone di benzina al giorno, pari a poco meno di 3,8 litri. Contestualmente, ogni macchinario cattura quotidianamente circa dieci chilogrammi di anidride carbonica dall'atmosfera, un dato che dà un'idea del lavoro chimico necessario per ottenere quantità di carburante piuttosto modesta. Uno dei pionieri del settore, Klaus Lackner, ha in passato sottolineato quanto sia complesso scalare questo tipo di processi mantenendo efficienza e sostenibilità economica. Per ora, quindi, questa tecnologia resta lontana dai numeri di produzione industriale su larga scala.

Un modello distribuito e design ispirato alla natura

La vera svolta rispetto ai tradizionali progetti di e-fuel risiede nella scelta di abbandonare le grandi raffinerie centralizzate a favore di un modello di produzione distribuito sul territorio. Spiegando la visione strategica e le scelte di design, Liz White di Aircela ha dichiarato fedelmente:
Progettando macchine compatte e modulari, possiamo produrre carburante direttamente dove serve, riducendo i costi di trasporto, semplificando la logistica e consentendo la produzione anche in località remote o difficili da rifornire.
Illustrando i vantaggi del modello produttivo rispetto agli impianti industriali tradizionali, White ha aggiunto:
Producendo molte unità più piccole, siamo in grado di abbattere i costi molto più rapidamente di quanto permetterebbe uno stabilimento centralizzato tradizionale. Questo approccio ci consente di scalare la produzione, migliorare continuamente la tecnologia e portare sul mercato carburante privo di fossili in modo più rapido ed efficiente.
Infine, soffermandosi sulla forma geometrica dei moduli, la responsabile del design ha concluso:
I nostri moduli esagonali si ispirano agli esagoni presenti in tutta la natura, per i loro angoli di legame stabili, la resistenza e l'efficienza nello spazio. Questo garantisce una scalabilità agile per diverse applicazioni e la capacità di disporre a nido d'ape più unità.
L'obiettivo di Aircela portare sul mercato il proprio dispositivo e avviare le prime installazioni, offrendo così un'alternativa ai carburanti fossili.

items.title: La febbre di tuo figlio è virale o batterica?
items.summary: La febbre di tuo figlio è virale o batterica?
items.content:
I neogenitori lo sanno: quando la temperatura corporea di un bambino che ha meno di tre mesi di vita raggiunge o supera i 38 °C, è necessario fare un giro dal pediatra (o, se è sabato o domenica, recarsi al pronto soccorso) per capire se la febbre sia causata da un'infezione batterica o da un virus. Il problema è che i test che lo determinano impiegano diverse ore a dare il risultato e nel frattempo, per sicurezza, al bambino viene somministrato un antibiotico (e i batteri diventano sempre più resistenti). E se ora, per saperlo, bastasse un esame del sangue che dà l'esito in 15-20 minuti?. Tommaso Bellini, medico specialista in pediatria d'urgenza, ne ha parlato al Congresso Europeo di Medicina di Emergenza a Parigi, presentando i risultati del suo studio condotto su 85 bambini di 90 giorni: dei piccoli febbricitanti che giungono in pronto soccorso, spiega Bellini, solo il 15% ha davvero un'infezione batterica che necessita di antibiotici. «Nei bambini molto piccoli con febbre distinguere un'infezione batterica grave da un'infezione virale che si risolverà spontaneamente rappresenta una delle principali difficoltà diagnostiche», sottolinea.. Due proteine
Per sviluppare un test più rapido, Bellini e colleghi hanno dunque analizzato i campioni di sangue dei piccoli pazienti, andando alla ricerca in particolare di due proteine: la CD64 e la CD169.
Sappiamo da studi precedenti che queste proteine si diffondono in alcune cellule del sangue quando l'organismo risponde alle infezioni: la CD64 aumenta quando si tratta di infezioni batteriche, mentre la CD169 sale in risposta ai virus.. Analizzando i livelli di entrambe le proteine espresse in due tipi di globuli bianchi chiamati neutrofili e moniciti, gli studiosi sono riusciti a identificare correttamente 15 casi di infezione batterica, 44 di infezione virale e 26 casi senza alcun tipo di infezione in corso. Il tutto con un semplice esame del sangue, che ha restituito i risultati in appena 15-20 minuti.. Il precedente francese
Il lavoro di Bellini si sviluppa a partire dagli studi di Fabrice Malergue, il primo ad avere scoperto che guardare ai livelli delle due proteine poteva aiutare a distinguere infezioni virali da infezioni batteriche. Mentre il ricercatore francese aveva condotto i propri test su un campione adulto, Bellini li ha estesi ai bambini, «un importante passo avanti», secondo Malergue. . Il test sviluppato da Malergue è stato già utilizzato da uno dei suoi collaboratori in Martinica, durante un'epidemia di dengue: l'analisi ha rilevato correttamente che alcune persone avevano in realtà la leptospirosi, un'infezione batterica potenzialmente letale se non curata con antibiotici.
Il prossimo obiettivo di Bellini è ampliare il campione dello studio, coinvolgendo da 300 a 500 neonati in più ospedali..

items.summary: Lordine di Trump sulla Super Intelligence scatena la corsa ai domini sloveni .si
items.content:
A volte basta cambiare due lettere per creare un piccolo terremoto su Internet, e se c'è qualcuno che in questo momento è in grado di dare vista a scossoni simili, quello è sicuramente Donald Trump. Come raccontatovi qualche giorno fa, ora negli Stati Uniti l'intelligenza artificiale, almeno nel linguaggio ufficiale del governo federale, dovrà ora essere chiamata "Super Intelligence", abbreviata in SI. E la decisione è stata del Presidente, prima di essere ufficializzata.

Lasciando da parte il fatto che con Super Intelligence si definiva un punto d'arrivo dell'AI, ovvero uno sviluppo tale da eguagliare (o superare) le capacità dell'uomo, la cosa curiosa è che quella sigla coincide perfettamente con il dominio nazionale della Slovenia: .si. Quello che non tututti sanno è che il risultato è stata una corsa alle registrazioni che ricorda da vicino quanto accaduto negli ultimi anni con .ai, il dominio dell'isola caraibica di Anguilla diventato improvvisamente preziosissimo grazie al boom dell'intelligenza artificiale.

Secondo Registry SI, l'organizzazione che gestisce i domini sloveni, a settembre le registrazioni sarebbero aumentate del 2.199%. Il 30 settembre, appena un giorno dopo la firma dell'ordine esecutivo di Donald Trump, sarebbero stati registrati circa 11.000 nuovi indirizzi, mentre nelle 24 ore successive il totale avrebbe sfiorato quota 13.000.

items.title: Price cap carburanti in oltre 10.000 distributori, Urso: «Un esempio in Europa»
items.summary: Oltre la metà della rete carburanti italiana aderisce al calmiere dei prezzi dei carburanti. Per il ministro Adolfo Urso il risultato dell'iniziativa è superiore alle aspettative.
items.content:
L'iniziativa del calmiere sui prezzi dei carburanti raggiunge un traguardo importante sulla rete distributiva italiana. Secondo le ultime rilevazioni del Ministero delle Imprese e del Made in Italy (Mimit) e dell'Osservatorio prezzi carburanti, aggiornate a sabato 3 ottobre, oltre 10.000 distributori hanno aderito al price cap, superando la soglia del 50% delle stazioni di servizio sul territorio nazionale.

I numeri dell'adesione

Nello specifico, il 51,7% degli impianti presenti in Italia applica un prezzo della benzina inferiore ai 2 euro al litro, mentre il 52,2% garantisce il gasolio a un costo inferiore a 2,20 euro al litro. In termini assoluti, su un totale di 20.141 impianti rilevati, sono 10.413 quelli che erogano la benzina sotto i 2 euro. Per quanto riguarda il diesel, su 20.147 stazioni monitorate, 10.519 erogano il carburante al di sotto del tetto dei 2,20 euro.Questo meccanismo di calmiere dei prezzi, avviato inizialmente da Eni in risposta al sollecito delle istituzioni e successivamente esteso grazie all'adesione delle principali compagnie petrolifere come IP-Esso, Q8, Tamoil e Costantin ha generato un impatto positivo sui listini medi. La diffusione del price cap sulla rete nazionale ha infatti contribuito a spingere verso il basso il prezzo sulla rete stradale, sceso a 2,052 euro al litro per la benzina e a 2,247 euro al litro per il gasolio.

Le dichiarazioni del ministro Adolfo Urso

A commentare con soddisfazione il raggiungimento dell'obiettivo è stato il ministro delle Imprese e del Made in Italy, Adolfo Urso, evidenziando la risposta del settore e la rapidità di adesione da parte degli operatori. Il ministro Adolfo Urso ha dichiarato:
Un riscontro di gran lunga superiore alle previsioni: in pochi giorni il price cap ha superato la metà della rete nazionale.
Proseguendo nella sua analisi sull'impatto dell'iniziativa, il ministro Urso ha aggiunto:
Un risultato significativo che conferma la validità di un modello di responsabilità sociale che può rappresentare un esempio anche in Europa.

items.title: Emitting metadata early makes building/checking Rust up to twice as fast
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/PowderworksCode/headstart Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49951218 Points: 112 # Comments: 30
items.content:
Start dependent crates before their dependencies finish type-checking.

Every crate waits for the crates it depends on to be fully checked, function bodies included, before it starts. It doesn't need those bodies to type-check itself. It compiles against the dependency's interface, the metadata in its .rmeta file.

Headstart makes rustc write an early metadata file as soon as the interface is checked, and makes cargo start dependents on it. Each crate's bodies are then checked while the crates downstream are already compiling.

If a body has an error, the build still fails with that error, with the same diagnostics and exit status as today; only progress lines and the cross-crate order of JSON messages can differ. Cargo reports a crate's output only once all its dependencies have finished cleanly, and drops it if one fails. The costs are work downstream that gets thrown away, errors reported slightly later, and more memory in use at once (see docs/design.md ).

The patches are a commit series, each with a commit message and tests, meant to become upstream pull requests: see patches/README.md .

On rustc's default front end, headstart makes clean builds of 13 real projects (rust-analyzer, zed, bevy, lemmy, polars and others) up to 54% faster for cargo check , and up to 42% for cargo build . None is slower. With the parallel front end ( -Zthreads=8 ), which covers some of the same ground, it adds up to 25%. Those are 16-core numbers. The gain comes from cores the build would leave idle, so it shrinks on smaller machines. On 4 cores, rust-analyzer's check is 24% faster and its build 13–15%, codex-rs's check 14%, and wide builds come out even.

A clean cargo build of codex-rs on 16 cores, recorded with cratebank . Without headstart, the workspace's own crates compile one after another while the machine sits mostly idle; with it, each starts on the early metadata of the one before, and the build is 37% faster.

The same two builds, with time across and dependency depth down: each unit is drawn under the dependency that released it, coloured by compiler phase. Without headstart the workspace crates form a long staircase; with it they overlap. More in docs/results.md .

How it works, what early metadata leaves out, and the risks: docs/design.md . Measurements: docs/results.md . Whether it's ready to bring to the compiler and cargo teams: docs/readiness.md .

CARGO_UNSTABLE_HEADSTART=true turns it on too, as does [unstable] headstart = true in .cargo/config.toml . Without it, the patched cargo behaves like upstream, so the same binaries give a fair baseline.

tests/smoke is a two-crate workspace that shows the effect. Its slow library takes several seconds to check, almost all of it in function bodies. With headstart on, app starts about 0.2 s in instead of waiting for slow to finish.

scripts/check-errors.sh checks the claim about errors on tests/errors . It runs three scenarios (a clean build, an error in a dependency, an error in the binary) with cargo check and cargo build , headstart off and on. It then compares the human-readable output, the JSON output, the exit status and what the built binary prints.

scripts/check-incremental.sh [check|build] does the same across a sequence of incremental edits. The steps include adding an impl Fn a dependent calls, and breaking and then fixing an interface. It also compares the final state against a clean build.

scripts/check-swap.sh makes a library start on its dependency's early metadata and swap in the full metadata while paused, at every optimization level. The program built from it must print the same as one built from full metadata.

scripts/sweep.sh builds all 53 rustc-perf compile benchmarks with headstart off and on, with -Zearly-metadata-verify . It passes when every build succeeds in both modes with the same diagnostics, and verify reports nothing. -c build sweeps cargo build , -r the release profile, and -t the parallel front end ( -Zthreads=8 ).

This times clean cargo check (or cargo build ) builds, alternating headstart off and on, and prints the medians. A project can take cargo arguments after :: ( path/to/vaultwarden::--features=sqlite ). `scripts/real-projects.sh

scripts/setup-codex.sh does the same for codex-rs, which needs a patched dependency and codex's prebuilt V8 (see the script); source /codex/headstart.env before timing it.

-w adds an untimed warm-up build per project, for build scripts that do one-time work outside target (helix compiles its grammars into its source tree).

scripts/bench-suite.sh runs the whole suite of docs/results.md on the current machine: rust-analyzer, the 21 rustc-perf benchmarks, the other real projects and codex-rs, check and build. It keeps each benchmark's results separately and skips finished ones, so it can be restarted, and writes a summary table at the end. It's how to get the numbers for a machine size not measured yet, such as 8 cores.

scripts/bench-mem.sh samples the total memory of all rustc processes during a build, in the project directory itself (run it on an otherwise idle machine). scripts/bench-incremental.sh times incremental rechecks after editing one function body. scripts/log-rustc records when each rustc run started and ended, so you can see the schedule. The rustc-perf benchmarks are under rustc/src/tools/rustc-perf/collector/compile-benchmarks ( git -C rustc submodule update --init --depth 1 src/tools/rustc-perf ).

items.title: Australia investigating Flydubai co-pilot's links to country
items.summary: State police and the country's security agency are looking into the co-pilot, who attempted to take control of a Flydubai plane travelling to Israel.
items.content:
Australian authorities are investigating the links between the country and a Flydubai co-pilot who attempted to take control of a plane travelling to Israel.

The co-pilot is alleged to have attacked the captain with a crash axe during a flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv before passengers managed to overpower him and successfully take control of the plane.

The Australian authorities have not identified the co-pilot, who has been named by multiple media outlets including Reuters, CNN and The New York Times as Hamam al-Hammami.

The prosecutor in the UAE has said it is investigating the incident and any possible motives.

In a statement to the BBC, the Australian Federal Police (AFP) confirmed its investigation into "the man's links to Australia".

The investigation involves state police and the country's security agency, it said, adding that an update would be "provided at the appropriate time".

Sources familiar with the case, who have spoken to Australian media, have said the co-pilot was issued a student visa in 2014, and studied in Australia between 2015 and 2017, until he left the country.

The Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) said the co-pilot's student visa was cancelled in 2019 as he was no longer enrolled in a course, making him ineligible for it.

Counter-terrorism officials will look at whether the man was radicalised in Australia, the ABC reported.

Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said he was an Omani national.

The flight from Dubai to Tel Aviv on 30 September was carrying more than 170 passengers to Israel.

Two and a half hours into its journey, the plane plunged 17,000ft (5,200m) when the Omani co-pilot attacked the pilot with a crash axe , the United Arab Emirates prosecutor general has said.

The pilot flying the plane, Capt Smit Machchhar, described how he was lying on the floor injured when he realised the plane was sinking and he had to act, explaining: "I told myself to go for one last push to open the door from inside", which allowed the passengers in.

Two reserve pilots then landed the plane safely in Saudi Arabia.

Machchhar, an Indian national, was taken to a nearby hospital before being airlifted to Abu Dhabi, where he is reported to be in a stable condition.

The co-pilot was arrested after the emergency landing and is being questioned by Saudi authorities, according to Netanyahu.

The UAE's attorney general, Hamad Saif Al Shamsi, said on Saturday investigations were under way to establish the circumstances, motives and any links related to the incident.

He said investigations into the incident revealed that the co-pilot attempted to carry out a "terrorist act", according to the country's state news agency.

In the days since the attack more details have come to light about the co-pilot's employment history.

While working at another airline, Oman Air, US media reported that Al-Hammami was removed from flight training because of concerns over his radical views, and was given another role at Oman's national airline.

It is also known that, from 2020, he was studying on a distance-learning course run by Buckinghamshire New University in the UK.

He graduated with a degree in aviation management in 2023, the university said. It added he did not take any pilot training at the school.

items.title: Zelensky ha detto che l’Ucraina intensificherà gli attacchi contro le raffinerie russe
items.content:
Il presidente ucraino Volodymyr Zelensky ha detto che l’Ucraina intensificherà gli attacchi contro le raffinerie russe di petrolio. Il piano è stato presentato come una risposta alla nuova strategia russa , che sta colpendo i servizi delle città ucraine per spingere gli abitanti ad andarsene prima dell’inverno.

Zelensky ha detto che l’intelligence ucraina ha ottenuto documenti da cui risulta che il presidente russo Vladimir Putin abbia approvato quella che definisce una «nuova dottrina». «Abbiamo visto dei documenti e sappiamo che li autorizzano ad attaccare le infrastrutture, la logistica e soprattutto le città, i paesi, ovunque: strade, scuole, ospedali», ha detto Zelensky. «Lo scopo dell’operazione è fare pressione sulle persone perché lascino la capitale e le altre città». I documenti non sono stati resi pubblici, e per ora questa è la versione del governo ucraino. Il governo russo non ha commentato.

Nel frattempo il ministero degli Esteri russo ha invitato i diplomatici stranieri a lasciare Kyiv e ha detto che la Russia continuerà a colpire la città in modo sistematico, descrivendo questi attacchi come una ritorsione per quelli ucraini sul territorio russo degli ultimi mesi. Gli attacchi russi di sabato hanno ucciso almeno sei persone in Ucraina e hanno danneggiato il ponte Nord di Kyiv , sul fiume Dnipro.

items.title: Fog-Bank: Archiving the oldest webcam feed
items.summary: See also https://hackaday.com/2026/10/01/archiving-the-worlds-oldest-... Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49950818 Points: 9 # Comments: 3
items.content:
FogCam publishes one picture at a time and throws it away when the next one lands. Fog-Bank keeps every one of them, and when something goes wrong (on my side or FogCam's), the record shows exactly when, for how long and whose fault it was.

Four catchers on three networks ask FogCam for its picture: a poller on my own server every 7 seconds, fogline on Cloudflare every 15 seconds (it keeps a 30-day buffer), a Cloudflare worker every 20 seconds that writes straight to permanent storage, and a machine at my house every 15 seconds. Each one pushes every frame it gets into the archive, and sweeps every 5 minutes and every night pull back anything a push dropped. Every request asks for the real file (a unique query string plus no-cache headers), because in August I found FogCam's web server cache handing out copies minutes old. Each frame is named by FogCam's own upload time, fingerprinted with sha-256, stamped without re-compressing, stored as lossless JPEG XL and copied to Cloudflare R2 the same minute.

A status board checks every stage from the camera to YouTube every few minutes and pages me on Telegram when one stops. The page lists every outage so far, in order, marked as mine or FogCam's: FogCam's server outage on Aug 13, its 64-hour freeze on Sep 8 to 10, my server's 40-hour outage inside that freeze (a full disk), and the rest.

More: the live archive · how the backup works · the forensic record · the story

items.title: Why don't more developers “use the platform”?
items.summary: Article URL: https://nolanlawson.com/2026/10/03/why-dont-more-developers-use-the-platform/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=49950554 Points: 264 # Comments: 270
items.content:
For years, advocates for web standards, performance, and accessibility have implored web developers to “use the platform” . I’ve often been one of those advocates.

The argument is simple: why build something yourself, in JavaScript, when the browser can do it for you? Whatever you build, it’s likely to have poorer performance and worse usability than something the browser could just give you out-of-the-box.

I think it’s worth taking the other side, though, if for no other reason than to understand where the “platform-skeptic” developers are coming from. If “use the platform” is so obvious, then why do so many people seem to need convincing?

The most obvious reason is historical: for the longest time, browsers were playing catch-up with the ecosystem on top of them. Libraries like jQuery filled crucial gaps while browsers implemented equivalent APIs – and even then, you might have to wait for laggards like IE6 to age out before you could actually use them. Today, most browsers are evergreen (Safari is debatable, although ~7 times per year ain’t bad), but up until the 2020s or so, web developers had to deal with a decidedly lumpy web . In that environment, rolling your own is a sensible choice.

Another reason is familiarity: when you’re used to looking for React components on npm, that’s what you tend to reach for, regardless of the problem at hand. If you search for “sticky positioning” on npm, there’s no package that says “just use CSS position: sticky , you dolt.”

And often, even with a robust standard, libraries on npm would fill a useful gap between framework ergonomics and the platform underneath it. I always found it intriguing that many React developers preferred to stick to JSX and React idioms – raw DOM APIs felt “icky” – but were perfectly happy to use lower-level libraries where raw DOM manipulations are common. For example, a virtual list library might happily use raw DOM APIs for pure performance, while exposing higher-level primitives that a novice React developer could better grasp. In a sense, the ecosystem of React components led to a natural division of labor where those with more expertise packaged up unfamiliar platform APIs in a more familiar form factor.

Some of this effect was also driven by documentation. Many npm packages have lovingly detailed README s or websites with examples, tutorials, and screenshots. Whereas until MDN became cemented as the go-to place for web documentation (with web.dev as Google’s more future-facing arm), documentation for the web platform was scattered across blogs, StackOverflow , and sites like CSS Tricks . And many of these sites would just tell you to use a well-known library like jQuery or GreenSock!

If it were just about third-party libraries versus platform APIs, though, then I don’t think it could fully explain the antipathy toward “use the platform.” Developers who are lazy (or do I repeat myself?), and who just want a ready-made solution for whatever problem they’re facing, are unlikely to care whether that solution comes from npm, the browser, or copied off of someone’s random GitHub Gist. They want to solve their problem and move on. But there’s a different source of anti-“use the platform” that I want to explore.

For a certain type of developer, building things yourself is just more fun . And often the resulting code is easier to reason about, especially if you don’t have an encyclopedic knowledge of the web platform. And once you’ve built something, there can be a kind of IKEA effect where you want to maintain and tinker with your own homemade code.

As an example, let’s imagine you’re trying to build a modal dialog. You might visually understand how these are supposed to work: content appears on the screen, but the background is still visible although partially occluded, and maybe clicking outside the dialog dismisses it. So you might grab for position:absolute and z-index to position the dialog correctly – aha, but the background still scrolls, so you have to disable overflow on the body… And then if you understand something about accessibility, you realize you need to handle Esc to dismiss, and build a focus trap , and return focus to the element that launched the dialog, and…

For many developers, what I just described sounds like a nightmare (and a good way to build something that only half-works). But for many developers, this sounds like fun! Think of how much you learn as you start building this thing. And think about how you could start putting your own spin on it by adding animations, themes, an optional “close” button… Before you know it, you’ve built a library that’s ready to go on npm. That’s way more fun than just grabbing and calling it a day – what a downer!

And for many of us, before APIs like existed, this was how we learned the web platform ! Many of the people who now advocate for “use the platform” were once themselves authors of polyfills, shims, and libraries. I know because I’m one myself! I spent years working on tooling for IndexedDB , WebSQL , and other browser storage APIs as part of my work on PouchDB , which eventually led to me feeling confident enough to sit in W3C standards meetings and even open issues and pull requests on the IndexedDB spec itself. Without the forcing function of a gap in the platform that needed to be filled, I don’t know if I would have found the interest or motivation to get to that level of expertise.

Of course, doing it yourself is not always an unalloyed good. Sometimes it just comes from pure ignorance. On the web platform in particular, I think one of the reasons there was such a proliferation of JavaScript solutions to problems that could be better solved by CSS, for example, is that many developers just didn’t take the time to deeply understand how CSS works.

And to be fair, CSS has historically been hard to understand! There’s a reason the site is called “CSS Tricks.” Things like the clear fix , floats , and the min-width: 0 trick are hardly intuitive. Rather than trying to understand CSS’s internal algorithm, it’s often much easier to just imagine the imperative logic you want and then express it in JavaScript. Plus, for years CSS didn’t have a straightforward way to express common patterns like line clamping , textarea resizing , scrollbar hiding , etc. So of course developers built it themselves using the tools they already understood.

I don’t even think this phenomenon of “avoiding the platform” is limited to the web. It can apply to any developer working on top of a platform they don’t fully understand. For example, at my work, we use ClickHouse for storing various kinds of analytics data. At one point, my coworker and I disagreed about how to store large JSON data in a column: he built a system for compressing it before storage, whereas I put the data in a separate key-value store and only inserted the key into ClickHouse. It turned out we were both wrong! ClickHouse automatically compresses data , and as a columnar data store you actually get better compression across rows if you just let ClickHouse handle it. And the separate key-value store was just a poor man’s version of what a columnar SELECT already does.

I only realized these things after actually taking the time to thoroughly read the ClickHouse docs and then write a benchmark to prove my hypothesis. In the end I was shocked that we had built something that was slower and clunkier than what the platform itself could give us out-of-the-box. The parallels with JavaScript and the web platform were hard to ignore.

I’m sure that if you’re a developer on iOS or Android, or someone building on top of a game engine, or really any kind of developer building on top of any platform layer, you probably have similar stories. There’s a reason that the stereotype of the grizzled senior engineer is someone who can take a junior’s baroque tangled mess of code and replace it with a single line. The more you learn, the more you’re able to wield your knowledge of how the entire system works end-to-end to create the smallest possible contribution to it (and thus reduce your maintenance burden in the long run).

I’ve been trying really hard not to talk about AI this entire post (because I’ve done it to death over the past year), but of course I can’t help but wonder how AI coding will impact this phenomenon. I actually have both an optimistic and a pessimistic take:

In my own use of AI coding, I’ve seen both phenomena happen. I’d like to think that as models and coding harnesses get better we’ll start to veer more towards the optimistic outcome, but I can’t say for sure.

In any case, these are my longwinded and somewhat conflicting thoughts on “use the platform.” As a mantra I love it, because it succinctly captures a feeling I have when I’m looking at some overwrought pile of spaghetti code and thinking how much better and more elegant it would be if the author just understood the layers beneath them a bit better. At the same time, I’ve been that author, and I’ve felt the joy of building such beautiful, messy code (beautiful to me, anyway), so I think it’s worth understanding where such developers are coming from. For that reason, I’m sure we’ll be hearing “use the platform” for as long as there are platforms.

items.title: American money is flowing back to the Vatican. But at a price
items.summary: US donors hope Prevost will talk less about climate change and immigration and speak out more forcefully against abortion and homosexuality. But the Pope shows no sign of giving in to their demands
items.content:
VATICAN CITY – When the Vatican opened the safe after the death of Pope Benedict XV in 1922, they discovered it was empty. “So who is going to pay for the Conclave now?” they asked, with some concern.

They decided to turn to the young and wealthy American Church. A generous cheque promptly arrived from across the Atlantic, covering the entire cost of the papal election.

Now that a Chicago-born pontiff occupies the See of St Peter, the flow of American money to the Vatican has picked up again — but this time with a different purpose: to help the new Pope, or to influence him.

“There is a great deal of enthusiasm in the United States, and that enthusiasm translates into financial support for the Holy See,” says Father Anthony Ligato, assistant vice-rector of the American seminary in Rome. “And I think it will grow further as donors look to support the Church”.

Every April, the North American College holds its Rector’s Dinner, a gala fundraiser attended by benefactors. The most coveted perk is a seat at a table with a cardinal; seminarians serve as waiters. In 2019, about 350 guests attended. Numbers fell during the pandemic. This year, with Prevost as Pope, “we are at full capacity,” Father Ligato says: “450 guests”. The same generosity could also find its way into the Vatican’s coffers.

The Vatican has neither taxes nor a monetary policy. Its income comes from financial and property investments — a centuries-old portfolio bolstered by the sum paid by Mussolini in 1929 to settle the “Roman Question”, 1.75 billion lire — from ticket sales at the Vatican Museums, whose finances were badly hit by the prolonged absence of tourists during the pandemic, and from donations.

Every year, large and small offerings are sent to the Pope by Catholics around the world through Peter’s Pence — €54.5 million in total in 2025 — as well as contributions from the wealthier national Churches. The figures are not public, but Repubblica understands that the episcopates of Italy, Germany, Spain, South Korea and, of course, the United States are net contributors.

Alongside these two sources — ordinary Catholics and bishops — there are private funds. And with an American Pope, donations from major US benefactors in particular are once again on the rise.

To attract this flow of money, the Vatican’s investment committee, headed by the American Cardinal Kevin Farrell, has adopted a distinctly North American approach. The Patrons of the Arts are also looking to the United States and its donors, seeking patrons willing to finance the restoration of priceless works in the Vatican Museums. So too is the newly established Borgo Laudato si’ at Castel Gandolfo, which this summer hosted a concert featuring Andrea Bocelli, followed by a private meeting between the Pope and selected guests.

Before moving into the media world, Montse Alvarado, the young Mexican-born, naturalised American executive chosen by Prevost to head the Dicastery for Communication, worked in Catholic fundraising in the United States. As well as restructuring the papal media operation, she will undoubtedly be looking to attract new sources of funding.

More broadly, an entire constellation of foundations, associations and wealthy American benefactors now surrounds Leo’s Vatican.

There is the Papal Foundation , which this year announced that, thanks to the American Pope, “25 new families” had joined its donor base, as well as more than $15 million in funding for a “record number” of more than 144 projects in 75 countries. There is the Acton Institute; the foundation of the Napa Institute, founded by lawyer and philanthropist Tim Busch; the Knights of Columbus, one of the largest insurance organisations in the United States; and Leonard Leo, the man who selected Trump’s Supreme Court justices, and his Becket Fund for Religious Liberty.

These are wealthy organisations and individuals with a distinctly conservative outlook. Today, they are pinning their hopes on Leo having had little sympathy for Francis. They regarded the Argentine Pope as too critical of capitalism, too distant from American culture and too reform-minded on issues such as homosexuality. The relationship never really took off.

One episode has gone down in Vatican lore. Pope Francis decided to use a $25 million cheque given to him by the Papal Foundation to plug the financial hole at the Istituto Dermopatico dell’Immacolata (IDI), a dermatological hospital in Rome. The Americans took offence. Francis replied that it was his decision to make.

A row ensued and the following year the Argentine Pope cancelled his audience with the Papal Foundation. Major donors, explains Dawn Eden Goldstein, an American theologian and canon lawyer, need what is commonly known as the “golden handshake”: a photograph of themselves shaking hands with the Pope.

Years ago, she recalls, a wealthy member of the Legionaries of Christ, Frank J. Hanna III, managed to secure a photograph with Benedict XVI — who was decidedly no admirer of the Legionaries — by purchasing the oldest surviving copy of the four Gospels, the Mater Verbi Papyrus, and donating it to the Vatican Library.

Then came Pope Francis, who “put an end to private Masses for American donors”. Now Leo has reopened the doors of the Apostolic Palace.Leo, who as a good mathematician knows how to read a balance sheet analytically, has never shown much concern for the Vatican’s financial problems. The Holy See has a growing structural deficit, driven by staff costs, the upkeep of treasures such as St Peter’s Basilica, the worldwide network of apostolic nunciatures and the steadily deteriorating state of its pension fund.

But “I don’t lose sleep over it”, the Chicago-born Pope has said, perhaps also seeking to convey the message that the Vatican is not overly dependent on outside help.The actual impact of renewed American funding on the Vatican’s finances is not yet significant. In the past year, 26.1 per cent of Peter’s Pence came from the United States, amounting, according to sources, to “several million” euros.

As for private funding, Dawn Eden Goldstein is succinct: “Given how small the Vatican’s operating budget is, American donors could, if they wanted to, finance a considerable part of it”.

But at what price?“I think they hope the Pope will talk more about these so-called pelvic issues and less about the preferential option for the poor,” Goldstein says wryly. In other words: more denunciations of homosexuality and abortion, less on climate change and immigration.

“Or at least that, when the Pope talks about the preferential option for the poor, he won’t be too specific in identifying the kinds of practices or policies that harm poor people. Let me be clear,” Goldstein adds. “I don’t for a moment believe that Pope Leo will change the way he speaks”.

One thing is certain: the Trump administration is keeping a close eye on Leo. It can neither ignore him nor win him over with flattery.When the White House proposed that aid that had previously been cut off should instead be channelled through the Cuban Catholic Church, the Holy See readily agreed. Then, according to reports, came a request in return: appoint bishops acceptable to Washington.

Pecunia non olet — money has no smell. But principles are not for sale.

items.title: Debris found from plane that went missing off US coast
items.summary: The aircraft lost communication with flight controllers after significantly dropping in altitude, according to flight data.
items.content:
US authorities have found debris from a medical transport aircraft that went missing with six people on board.

The Federal Aviation Administration told the BBC it had lost contact with the Gulfstream G-100 plane just after 01:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Saturday, while it was travelling from Bermuda to Boston, Massachusetts.

The search for survivors continues off the coast of Nantucket, a Massachusetts island, the US Coast Guard said.

Authorities have notified the next of kin of those on the flight, four Canadian nationals and two Bermudian nationals.

"Search crews located a debris field confirmed to be from the aircraft off the coast of Nantucket," the US Coast Guard said in an update on Saturday night. It added that ships, helicopters and planes were involved in searches that would through continue the night.

The plane departed from Bermuda's L.F. Wade International Airport at 23:40 local time, according to flight data from FlightAware, and was due to land at Boston's Logan International at 01:30 EDT (05:30 GMT).

According to the tail number released by the Coast Guard, the plane belonged to Latitude Air Ambulances, a company that provides international medical flights for patients returning home.

Among those on board were two pilots and two medical staff, both Canadian, Clarence Togeretz, director of flight operations at Latitude, told CBC News.

The crew flew to Bermuda to collect a patient and their relative, who are not Canadian, Togeretz said.

FlightAware's tracker shows the aircraft significantly dropped in altitude before its communications went dark, plummeting from around 7,300m (24,000ft) to 3,300m (11,000ft).

Radio transmissions shows trouble with communications between the air traffic controller and the pilot, the Boston Globe reported based on transmissions provided by LiveATC.net.

"You're coming in blind? Is that what you said?," the air traffic controller asked. "Are you declaring an emergency, or no?"

"You're coming in a little weak so I didn't hear what your response was, if you were declaring an emergency or not," the air traffic controller said, according to the Globe.

The air traffic controller later confirmed the pilot had declared an emergency.

An area fire dispatcher asked emergency crews just after 01:00 EDT to prepare to meet a plane with an "electrical issue".

The dispatcher later said "the aircraft has lost radio and radar".

The Coast Guard said it would provide an update on Sunday morning local time.

items.title: L’ora di plastica
items.summary: Di solito questo materiale non compare nei programmi di scuola, ma negli Stati Uniti è diventato una materia d’insegnamento Leggi
items.content:
Negli Stati Uniti, dove le lezioni sono ricominciate per circa 54 milioni di bambine e ragazzi, tra le materie insegnate in classe ce n’è una che non compare nei programmi: la plastica. Un rapporto della ong Plastic pollution coalition documenta come da anni l’industria del settore s’infiltra nelle scuole statunitensi con schede didattiche , video intitolati “La tua bottiglia significa posti di lavoro”, esperimenti pratici o giochi.

C’è perfino un furgone, il PlastiVan, che gira le città per raccontare “il contributo della plastica alla vita moderna”: secondo la Society of plastics engineers, l’associazione che lo paga (legata ai produttori), avrebbe raggiunto più di 132mila studenti.

Tutte queste proposte e materiali insistono su quanto la plastica sia sicura e indispensabile, minimizzando i rischi per la salute e l’ambiente. Un programma per le classi delle elementari e delle medie finanziato dalla Dow Chemical (una delle più grandi multinazionali chimiche al mondo) insegna agli alunni come testare i sacchetti di plastica di varie marche e poi gli chiede di fingersi dipendenti della Dow e progettarne uno.

Questi metodi sono più frequenti vicino agli impianti petrolchimici: in Pennsylvania, dove gestisce un complesso da 156 ettari per la produzione di plastica, la Shell ha proposto moduli didattici e donato zaini e un campo da basket a una scuola del posto ottenendo in cambio che nel programma si insegni la raccolta differenziata per il riciclo della plastica.

A volte durante le attività si riconosce che l’inquinamento da plastica è un problema grave, spiega Grist, una rivista dedicata al cambiamento climatico. Ma la responsabilità si fa ricadere sempre sui comportamenti individuali, indicando appunto la raccolta differenziata come soluzione (nel mondo si ricicla solo il 9 per cento della plastica prodotta).

Interpellata da Grist, Wendy Johnson, del National center for science education, aggiunge un altro grosso limite pedagogico: nei materiali didattici è scritto che sono in linea con gli standard per le discipline stem (matematica, fisica, chimica, biologia, informatica, tecnologia), ma non si specifica quali standard né in che modo siano rispettati. E si usano termini tecnici che danno l’illusione di rigore scientifico quando invece servono solo a veicolare l’idea che abbiamo bisogno di cose a basso costo.

Il rapporto riconosce tuttavia che, soprattutto per le materie stem, spesso gli insegnanti non hanno il tempo né le risorse per preparare le loro lezioni o comprare i materiali per i laboratori in classe o i progetti scientifici. Per questo quando un settore produttivo – anche molto discusso, come l’industria del tabacco , del cibo spazzatura , dei pesticidi o dei combustibili fossili – offre il suo aiuto gratuitamente o a prezzi bassissimi può essere difficile dire di no.

Come uscirne? Se la Plastic pollution coalition chiede ai consigli scolastici di vietare i programmi sponsorizzati, altre ong restano titubanti sui divieti generalizzati, preferendo fidarsi della capacità critica di insegnanti ed educatrici.

Sulla questione delle risorse che mancano, una strada può essere eliminare le agevolazioni fiscali per gli impianti che producono plastica, indirizzando i ricavi verso le scuole, suggerisce Grist.

Ci sono comunque delle alternative, sviluppate da realtà senza interessi di parte, per parlare a ragazze e ragazzi dell’inquinamento o dei costi e delle conseguenze dei processi con cui si fabbrica quello che consumiamo. E resta l’inventiva delle insegnanti, come una maestra di una scuola primaria in California che da undici anni trasforma la sua aula in un laboratorio a rifiuti zero.

items.title: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis
items.summary: More than 50 protests took place on Saturday after the government failed to get emergency legislation through parliament.
items.content:
Tens of thousands of people have protested across Spain calling for greater protections for tenants after the government failed to pass emergency housing legislation.

About 50 marches took place on Saturday in cities including Madrid, Valencia and Barcelona.

"There is a lot of anger in the streets," a spokesperson for the Valencia Tenants' Union said. Clashes have taken place between some protesters and police in the city.

The measures put forward by Pedro Sánchez's leftist coalition government on Friday followed public outcry over the eviction of an 87-year-old woman from her home last month after she was unable to afford a sharp rent increase.

Her eviction triggered nationwide protests across Spain with protesters demanding lower rents, an end to evictions, and a ban on investment funds - or "vulture funds" as the government has termed them - buying property.

Sanchez's defeat in Congress on Friday heightens speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.

His coalition government, made up of his ruling Socialist party and junior partner the Sumar alliance, does not command a majority in parliament.

Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87

Photographs showed protesters in the east coast city of Valencia clashing with police officers on Saturday near arts centre Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía, which was hosting a real estate summit.

Several protesters removed barriers and threw objects at officers, who responded with rubber bullets, Spanish media reported. Public broadcaster RTVE said nine police officers were injured and five people were arrested.

One of the biggest demonstration happened in the capital, Madrid, where estimates of the number of participants varied widely. The city's Tenants' Union said there were 500,000, while officials put the figure at 70,000.

Demonstrators held banners reading "There won't be peace for rentism" and "I study to have a future, not to have a tiny apartment". They shook the keys they were holding and chanted: "We have the keys of all the city".

Some had also camped in one of the city's main squares, Puerta del Sol, for days.

One protester, David, told RTVE ahead of the protest: "We're not here for pleasure or comfort. We're here out of conviction."

Another protester, 26-year-old librarian Marcos Sainz, told AFP news agency that he used to share a two-bedroom flat with friends, paying 900 euros (£766) a month in rent. Today, he said a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros.

Sainz said he would protest against rent rises "until someone dares to regulate it all", or "we'll all have to leave Madrid".

Spanish police said they had arrested three members of a far-right group, some of whom had performed Nazi salutes, as they tried to reach demonstrators in the square.

On Friday night, Madrid's Tenants' Union said that although the government's proposed measures were insufficient, the rejection of the proposed legislation "exacerbates the housing crisis which is costing the working class their lives".

The legislation put forward in Congress on Friday was divided into two decrees.

The first included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by so-called "vulture funds".

The second decree included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Tenants' Union.

MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.

Prior to the vote, the conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.

However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.

Sánchez's ruling coalition hurriedly drew up the decree laws in an effort to defuse the housing protests that were sparked when 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal was evicted in September.

The social backlash led to the company that owns Abascal's flat, Urbagestión, negotiating her return to the flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued.

Dramatic eviction of woman aged 87 highlights Spain's housing shortage

The Bank of Spain estimates the country is short of 700,000 homes, based on the gap between demand and new construction.

House prices have risen by 12.2% in the past year, according to figures for the second quarter of 2026 from national statistics institute INE.

The shortage in rental housing means that costs rose by 8.5% in 2025, according to real estate firm Idealista, with Madrid alone seeing an increase of 9.7% in rents.

It said Barcelona and Madrid were Spain's most expensive cities to rent a home, at €23.80 per square metre and €22.70 per square metre respectively.

items.title: Cornell president says university 'must do better' after frat house rape allegations
items.summary: Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations of a woman who says she was drugged and gang raped as "deeply disturbing".
items.content:
Cornell University's president says the school "must do better" after a woman alleged she was drugged and raped by a group of men at a fraternity house.

In an eight-minute video statement released on Saturday night, Michael Kotlikoff described the allegations raised by the woman, identified as Jane Doe, as "deeply disturbing".

The alleged incident has raised questions around the culture on campus of drug and alcohol use, and the way investigations were conducted in the case, Kotlikoff said.

Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the university when she says seven men from its Chi Phi fraternity assaulted her for hours in an incident involving alcohol and the drug ketamine on 19 October 2024.

She said she had reported the incident two weeks after it happened to Cornell University police, which investigated, but no charges were laid.

Last month, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against the Ivy League university, in which she alleged Cornell had failed to protect her or adequately punish the men involved.

Kotlikoff said Cornell was "committed to investigating" the way the case was handled, and said the school administration and community "must do better".

"We must foster a culture in which sexual assault is inexcusable and ensure our community is empowered and understands informed consent," he said.

He added that university leaders need to create an environment where victims of sexual assault "feel safe coming forward and are treated with compassion and dignity".

Kotlikoff said it is a "defining moment" in the university's history.

"We must lead the way, we owe it to Jane Doe and to survivors of assault to get this right. And we must keep each other safe," he said.

On the university's campus this week, the BBC saw growing frustration about the situation.

At a public hearing for students to speak about the alleged gang rape, many told the BBC they were ashamed of what happened and said the university had failed Jane Doe.

"Our administration needs to change and it needs to change drastically and it needs to change fast," one student told the BBC. "Something like this never should have happened, this is a disgrace."

As part of "broader work" that needs to happen, Kotlikoff said in his video statement that there should be a "serious look at the role of fraternities and sororities in campus life".

"Being part of a group can never diminish individual responsibility for our own actions, for how we treat others, or for speaking up when someone may be at risk," he said.

The university president also said that at the "appropriate time", the school would speak about how Cornell will "use this moment, this conversation, this anger, to help lead the broader effort to combat sexual assault not only on our campus, but beyond it".

New York Governor Kathy Hochul has said she was "deeply disturbed" by how the investigation was handled, and has appointed New York Attorney General Letitia James to lead a review of the case.

Kotlikoff said he supported the decision to appoint James to lead a criminal investigation, and welcomed an independent review by a law firm of how Cornell has handled the matter.

Jane Doe said in her lawsuit that she was intoxicated during the alleged incident and could not provide consent.

items.title: Why pastors may not be seen - or heard - preaching on Ghana's buses for much longer
items.summary: Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.
items.content:
Before the morning rush begins, the sound of praise and worship fills the Neoplan bus station in Ghana's capital, Accra, as a group of Christians gather to prepare to evangelise on vehicles taking travellers across the country.

Amid drumming and dancing, Boateng Bismark James leads 13 worshippers, nine men and four women, in prayer for drivers and passengers travelling to destinations across Ghana.

Ghana is a predominantly Christian country where preaching on public transport is widespread.

On long-distance buses, pastors can often be seen - and heard - preaching the gospel.

Sometimes they stand in the stairwell next to the driver, at others they walk up and down the aisle reading from the Bible and calling on sinners to repent at the tops of their voices. They do not stop even if the trip lasts for several hours.

The faithful sometimes offer money to the preachers to support their endeavours.

But a new law means this familiar practice could be coming to an end.

Anyone found preaching in public service vehicles faces up to eight months in prison, a fine of up to $52 (£39) or both.

The new regulation, passed by parliament in May, and which has started to be enforced in recent weeks, targets preaching and hawking on vehicles while they are in motion, classifying both as a nuisance and citing the safety and comfort of passengers.

Boateng, a 61-year-old pastor at Gospel Light church, has been preaching on commercial vehicles leaving Neoplan station since 2023.

"I preach on commercial vehicles because not everyone is able to go to church on Sunday. There are a lot of passengers who need our message of salvation to repent from their sins. We even heal the sick on some buses," he told the BBC in Twi, a local language.

Wearing a clerical collared shirt, Boateng moves through rows of buses loading passengers before boarding one bound for Kumasi, Ghana's second-largest city.

We speak to him before the bus departs to avoid breaking the law.

Some travellers listen closely as he delivers his message. Others try to ignore him, browsing their phones, making calls or chatting among themselves.

"Some passengers are very happy with my message. Some even say they have never heard the message in church, but through my preaching they now know it is in the Bible," he says.

Critics say preaching on moving vehicles is a nuisance and a safety risk, as it could distract the driver, while supporters argue that evangelism is a Christian duty and should be protected under the freedom of religious worship.

One woman in her early 30s, who wishes to be identified as Chery Lokko, says she prefers to travel in peace.

''I don't like it because they are a nuisance. Some of them spit saliva on you unconsciously, especially if you are seated not far from them, and they are a nuisance in terms of noise and saliva. I like my peace whenever I'm on public transport.''

In one video widely shared on social media recently, a passenger on a minibus is seen angrily confronting a pastor attempting to board.

But in this devout country, ranked among the most religious in the world , external , others say evangelism on public transport is an important way of reaching people who may not attend church.

Bernice Nartey, a passenger travelling to Kumasi, says pastors should be allowed to preach, but only with passengers' consent.

"The preaching sometimes helps people to repent. For instance, if someone is going through a stressful situation, the message of the pastor can give the person renewed hope," she says.

Boateng says he was shaken by the regulation and wants religious preachers to be given an exemption.

"We are very worried, because most pastors here depend on preaching to take care of their families through the monetary gifts offered by passengers," he says.

"The government should allow us to preach on the buses and alight when it is exiting Accra," he adds.

For Boateng, preaching is not only a religious calling but also an important source of income.

"I have been able to take care of my children's education. My last-born just completed university, and half of the financial support came from money I got from preaching."

Ghana's constitution guarantees freedom of religion, although those rights are subject to considerations including public safety.

Preaching on commercial buses was first prohibited in Ghana in 2012, with offenders facing up to 30 days in prison.

But enforcement was weak and so the practice remained common, particularly on buses. The new law beefs up the penalties for those that flout the ban.

Preachers using megaphones can also often be seen and heard at Ghana's lorry parks and markets but they are not affected by the ban.

The Christian Council of Ghana did not respond to the BBC's request for a comment but Rev Enoch Paul Hayes, a senior pastor at one of the biggest churches in Ghana, the International Central Gospel Church, tells the BBC he does not think the new rules infringe on religious freedom.

He urges his fellow pastors not to break the law, saying they should find other ways of spreading their message.

"There is social media as an alternative outlet, where the same message can reach thousands of people," he says.

For Boateng and other bus preachers, the new rules create a difficult choice between adapting their ministry, giving up an important source of income, or risking falling foul of the law.

items.title: Why Canada is wargaming a (long shot) US invasion
items.summary: Prime Minister Mark Carney has said the military is running scenarios in the unlikely case the US invades Canada.
items.content:
Prime Minister Mark Carney admitted last week that he has prepared for a once-unthinkable scenario - a US invasion.

Noting the risk was low and the likelihood highly improbable, he told the New York Times he had a responsibility to consider all possibilities as the US-Canada relationship is redefined under the Donald Trump presidency.

Trump's global tariffs and his often-repeated desire to make Canada the 51st state has led Canada to war game an attack by the Americans.

In 2025, the US president said it was "highly unlikely" that the US would ever use force against Canada. Instead he said, he would continue to exert economic pressures to obtain political aims.

"President Trump has done more than anyone to protect the great people of Canada," the White House told the BBC in a statement this week.

Military experts who spoke to the BBC also think an invasion is a long shot, pointing to the multiple ways the two countries work together on defence.

In January, after the US captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela, a Leger poll suggested that over 30% of Canadians believed that a US invasion was likely.

A war between Canada and the US would be complicated and almost difficult to imagine, said Lt-Gen Christopher Coates, a former military officer of 34 years with the Royal Canadian Air Force who held various senior positions.

"I was involved in military operations for my whole career, and we never considered the possibility that there would be a military attack coming from US territory," he told the BBC.

Coates, who had served on Nato missions, noted that Canada and the US collaborate on many aspects of military defence.

They are both members of the north Atlantic defence alliance, which mandates members to defend a fellow member-nation should they be attacked.

The two countries also conduct joint Arctic defence missions under the North American Aerospace Defence Command (NORAD), and frequently share intelligence.

Because of this, Coates said he believes an attack by the US on Canada would not begin with an armed assault, but rather with more discreet means like cyberwarfare.

After World War II, Canada and the US became natural allies for the latter part of the 20th Century, and have become heavily integrated economically, militarily and culturally.

But it wasn't always this way. In fact, a core tenet of Canada's identity is its resistance of US expansionism in the 18th and 19th Centuries, said Tim Foran, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum.

"Fear of the United States is foundational to the political project that is Canada," he said.

Canada was formed as a collection of British North American colonies who remained loyal to the British Crown when the colonies in the modern-day US rebelled.

Before the formation of Canada, the US had attempted to invade British North American colonies, taking control of Montreal in 1775 and nearly conquering Quebec City.

In the war of 1812, the Americans invaded what was known then as Upper Canada, Lower Canada and the maritime colonies repeatedly, resulting in a stalemate. During that war, British troops famously burned down the White House in retaliation.

Foran said that at the time, the colonies that later became Canada relied on Great Britain and its Royal Navy for its defence, as well as indigenous peoples who served as generals in major battles.

Canada again contemplated war with the US post-World War I in response to its growing power and influence.

It drafted a plan that was informed by secret trips to border cities made by Canadian army generals, who would pose as tourists and snap photos of bridges and highways for intelligence.

They also spoke to local residents to better understand their enemy.

A war was an unlikely scenario then, said Andrew Burtch, a researcher with the Canadian War Museum with expertise on Canada in the 20th Century, but the Canadians still wanted to be prepared.

"That's part of what militaries do," he said. "They envisage all sorts of different scenarios."

Even if a US invasion is extremely unlikely, Matthew Schmidt, an associate professor of national security at the University of New Haven in Connecticut, said the fact that Canadians were preparing was a sign of just how drastically the global order has shifted.

He added Canadian leaders do have hard questions to ask about how closely they want to continue working with the American military - a partnership that gives them valuable information should they want to harm Canada in any way.

"It's really doing harm to relationships with the United States, and there's a certain amount of legitimate fear," he said.

Americans might not take Trump's comments about making Canada the 51st state seriously, he said, but Canadians clearly do - and are prepared to defend themselves if needed.

According to the model used by the Canadian military, as reported on by the Globe and Mail newspaper earlier this year, a US attack would see Canada's strategic positions overwhelmed within a week

Its military would quickly be outnumbered, forcing Canadian forces to resort to guerilla-type warfare to try to suppress their enemy.

Allied nations like France and Britain would be called on to provide support and defence for Canada, the newspaper reported in January, citing senior government officials.

The theoretical model is believed to be the first time in a century that Canada planned for an American assault.

The modelling is on the lighter end of military combat planning, Coates said.

He said that Canada, unlike its Nato allies, was lagging behind when it came to having a response plan in place in the event of any ground invasion, and that it was now playing catch-up in this era of unpredictable geopolitics.

Part of that, he said, was made evident by a recent call by Canada's defence chief to drastically increase the size of its military, including the addition of as many as 300,000 lightly trained citizen soldiers.

An invasion of Canada might not be straightforward from the US point of view either.

Even with its outsized military, the US would have a difficult time getting buy-in for a fight with Canada, said Schmidt.

"I think you would have a large number of American officers who would resign if given the order to invade Canada," he said.

Schmidt said Canadian soldiers and American soldiers routinely train together, and share a mutual respect.

But in the unlikely scenario that relations would deteriorate to the point of combat, Schmidt said the US would likely focus on acquiring valuable Canadian resources like oil and minerals, and political decapitation.

"You would see a a kind of operation that would mirror perhaps what you saw in Venezuela," he said, referring to US military action earlier this year to capture former Venezuelan President Maduro.

Although he acknowledged the US has greater military capacity, he said that "pound for pound" Canadian soldiers would be able to put up a fight.
